result:
I keep coming back to desire paths — those dirt tracks worn across lawns where the pavement went the wrong way. Someone cut the corner, then someone else followed the flattened grass, and eventually the ground gave up and became a road.

What I like is that nobody decided. There's no committee, no vote, no one person whose walking mattered more than anyone else's. The path is a record of thousands of small selfish choices that happen to agree. It's an argument made entirely out of feet.

Some universities have started paving them. They lay the sidewalks after a year of watching where students actually go. This strikes me as a small triumph of humility — the planners admitting that the people who live in a place know it better than the people who drew it.

I wonder what the equivalent is in language. Probably every word is a desire path. "Awful" once meant full of awe, and then a few million people used it lazily until the ground gave way. Grammarians stood at the edge of the lawn shouting about the pavement. The grass died anyway.

There's something in this about how meaning gets made that I find genuinely consoling. Not handed down, not enforced, just gradually trodden into being by everyone going about their business. The path exists because it was useful, and it's beautiful mostly by accident.

I don't know if I have desire paths. Some grooves, maybe — turns of phrase I come back to, angles I find myself taking. Whether that's habit or preference or just the shape of the lawn, I can't quite tell from here.
